title: Surgical Win
summary: Keep the king off checking squares until the pawn sacrifice creates a winning race.

nodes.question: Push the pawn now, or improve the king route?
nodes.explanation: White must create a passed h-pawn without allowing the c-pawn to gain a decisive checking tempo.

nodes.question: Is it finally time to sacrifice f4?
nodes.explanation: The king has reached d1 by the light squares b3 and c2. The c-pawn cannot drive it away with a checking advance.

branches.title: Follow the light squares, then sacrifice
commentary: Begin from the complete six-piece source board. Pawn races depend on the king’s route as well as the number of steps to promotion.
Kb3 approaches the c-pawn while avoiding b4, where ...c5 would arrive with check.
c5 starts Black’s passed-pawn race. It does not check the king on b3.
Kc2 continues along light squares and prepares to meet the advancing c-pawn without losing a checking tempo.
c4 advances again, hoping to force the king into an awkward approach.
Kd1 keeps the king on a light square. White delays the pawn sacrifice until it can block the c-pawn from the correct side.
c3 is the source’s attempt to keep the king on b6 while racing the pawn toward promotion.
f5 now sacrifices a pawn at the favorable moment, drawing the g-pawn away from the h-pawn’s file.
gxf5 accepts and creates Black’s second passer, but it also leaves the h-pawn free to advance.

Kc2 blocks c2 and threatens to collect c3. White can coordinate against the two black passers while the h-pawn runs; this exact position is a White win. The branch stops at the checked blockade, without assuming a particular further Black move.

branches.title: Sacrifice before improving the king
commentary: Compare the immediate pawn sacrifice with the king still on a4.
f5 gives away the forced win. The h-pawn becomes passed, but the king has not reached the required defensive route.
gxf5 accepts. Black’s c-pawn and new f-pawn give enough counterplay to draw this exact position; a passed h-pawn alone does not establish a win.

branches.title: Approach on a checking square
commentary: Compare the source’s more direct king approach before the c-pawn advances.
Kb4 gives away the win because it allows Black to gain a checking tempo.
c5+ checks the king on b4, making White spend a move responding before it can continue toward the c-pawn.
Kc3 answers the check, but the exact position is drawn. The source’s first-move Kb3 avoids the checking tempo and preserves the winning route.

branches.title: Step onto c3 instead of c2
commentary: Compare a different king route after the correct first move.
Kb3 preserves the win by avoiding the immediate pawn check.
c5 continues the pawn race without check.
Kc3 gives away the win. White’s king has stepped onto a dark square where the later pawn advance can gain a checking tempo.
Kc6 is the source’s waiting defense. Black keeps the pawn timing flexible, and this exact position is drawn with best play.

exercises.prompt: Why care about the colors of the king’s squares?
exercises.answer: In this setup, b3, c2 and d1 avoid the c-pawn’s checking advances at the crucial moments. The useful rule is the exact tempo pattern, not that one color is always better.

exercises.prompt: Why wait until Kd1 before playing f5?
exercises.answer: The king can then return to c2 to stop c3 without first being displaced by a pawn check. That leaves time to handle the other passer while h4 runs.

startContext: Begin from the full six-piece opening diagram. The selected route is Kb3–c2–d1 before f5; three comparisons show why earlier pawn pushes or different king squares give away the win. Source pawn races beyond the checked blockade remain context.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
